arxiv:2611.15777.text: SO-Arena: Benchmarking the Capability Spectrum and Reliability of System One Models. From Lichen Li and colleagues. Fast System One models aim to make decisions without generating long chains of text, but broad scores can hide where they succeed and when their choices are dependable. SO-Arena tests these models across eleven domains and five capability families, including interactive tasks, and checks how stable their choices are when options change or none is valid. Across twenty-one models, scaling and extra reasoning helped unevenly across domains. The top model for overall performance ranked only seventh in reliability, showing that capability and trustworthiness need separate evaluation.

arxiv:2611.16748.text: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models. From Yuxuan Chen and colleagues. Video generators can create realistic scenes but often get physical motion and cause and effect wrong, while reliable training feedback is hard to obtain. PhysLoop guides language models through making, judging, and correcting videos, using their physics knowledge to build training data and repair clips. The team releases a collection of one hundred thousand videos, tools, and two evaluation datasets. Tests cover controllable generation, local repairs, and physical behavior on an external benchmark.

arxiv:2611.17167.text: Actor, Judge, or Teacher? Understanding Decision Models in Long-Horizon Agents. From Haochen Liu and colleagues. Long-horizon agents can struggle when they must complete a necessary subgoal before an easier one, raising the question of whether a model that acts poorly can still teach. Researchers compared decision models and general language models as actors and judges, then used one decision model to teach policies on ALFWorld and WebShop. The models often chose the easier subgoal, yet as judges they recognized steps toward the necessary one, especially when asked whether an action helped. Teaching with JEV improved success over the baseline on both tasks.

arxiv:2611.15131.text: Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction. From Hengyuan Cao and colleagues. Real-time assistants often treat reasoning as a control outside the simulated world, rather than part of it. Duo v1 introduces a model that combines intent, or deciding how to respond, with realization, or producing audio and visual behavior, on a shared timeline. It continuously takes in audio, video, and text while responding, and can handle spontaneous conversation and interruptions. This approach also supports interacting with real objects, changing virtual scenes, guiding assistants, and playing audiovisual games without a mouse or keyboard.

arxiv:2611.15844.text: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception. From Arpit Jadon and colleagues. Turning image generators into general vision systems can work, but the data and methods behind Vision Banana were not public. Open Vision Banana offers a reproducible approach, testing how color, prompts, model tuning, and task balance affect performance. Using open models and public training data, it beats Vision Banana's reported zero-shot result on Cityscapes and approaches leading depth estimators. A test-time method that combines segmentations from different color legends improves accuracy further, and the team releases its data pipeline, code, and model checkpoints.

arxiv:2611.17060.text: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors. From Hao Li and colleagues. Robots controlled by large models still struggle with long tasks that involve frequent contact with objects. Ropedia Xperience Two provides data to study how robot skills improve as environments and behaviors scale. It includes one thousand five hundred eighty-nine three-dimensional scene scans and four thousand two hundred thirty recordings of people performing seventy-four tasks. The captures can also be turned into interactive simulations and robot motion, creating reusable data for training and testing.

arxiv:2611.17331.text: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models. From Chin-Yang Lin and colleagues. Decoder-only view synthesis models can render new camera views at high quality, but their attention-based decoding is costly, while faster test-time training can reduce quality. Test-Time Baking teaches a small neural network to copy the useful mapping from cross-view attention, and separates camera information from image content to make that learning easier. It reaches up to twenty-three times faster rendering while maintaining quality on par with state-of-the-art methods across several benchmarks.

arxiv:2611.10649.text: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations. From Lorenz K. Muller and colleagues at Huawei Technologies. Low-precision weights and activations can make neural networks cheaper to run, but existing quantization methods may need costly optimization and model-specific changes. MACaQ quantizes each layer independently, using activation transforms and a procedure that adjusts individual weight codes to reduce error. It achieves lower perplexity than two competing methods, and matches their best result on Llama three eight B while taking eleven times less time. It also quantizes a one hundred twenty-two billion parameter model in sixty-four minutes using thirty-two point five gigabytes of graphics memory.

arxiv:2611.12870.text: SWAM: Scaling World Action Models with Cross-Modal Alignment. From Yu Zhou and colleagues. World action models learn to predict video and actions from language, but action training can weaken their understanding of how language relates to video. SWAM studies how different data and supervision choices affect that alignment, using a pool of about forty-seven thousand hours of videos and demonstrations. Under a fixed training budget, mixing first-person videos with UMI demonstrations improves control generalization, and the chosen model and training setup achieve stronger results on both simulated and real-world tasks.

arxiv:2611.16217.text: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It? From Zhiyu Hou and colleagues. WorldDraft tackles a challenge in using video models to render worlds built by code: keeping the planned motion and camera views while consistently showing the requested appearance. It tests twelve models on four hundred and thirty-two paired cases, varying how detailed the draft is and whether its visual cues agree with the requested look. The models struggle to preserve world structure and appearance together; richer drafts can also hurt visual fidelity. The proposed prompting method improves both goals across the tested video renderers.

arxiv:2611.13028.text: GTAGym: AAA Game Tasks Environment for Evaluation and Reinforcement Learning. From Jiajun Chen and colleagues. Testing agents in large commercial games is difficult because task success is hard to verify automatically, which also limits reinforcement learning. GTAGym provides a framework for testing and training agents on Grand Theft Auto Five, with a benchmark of story missions and image-based shooting tasks, plus automatic checks of outcomes. The best tested setup reached 70.9 percent accuracy on tasks where instructions appeared only at the start, though aerial navigation and evasion remained difficult. Training on generated tasks improved performance on native game tasks from 15 percent to 23 percent.

arxiv:2611.14815.text: BirdDreams: Joint Perspective and BEV Video Generation for a Plausible, Reactive Driving World Model. From Junyoung Seo and colleagues. Driving world models need to predict surrounding traffic while following a chosen path for the ego vehicle, but perspective video can hide vehicles and make their motion hard to learn. BirdDreams predicts camera video together with a simple top-down view of roads and vehicles, letting each view guide the other. It can steer the simulated scene using the top-down view and starts from a single camera image, without a high-definition map or vehicle-state inputs. Tests show more faithful path following than prior models, and people judged its surrounding-vehicle behavior more realistic than a perspective-only baseline.

arxiv:2611.16905.text: Factored One-sided Adam-Moment for Practical and Scalable SOAP. From Jaemyung Yu and colleagues. Large language model training can benefit from second-order optimizers, but methods like SOAP use substantial memory and computation. Factored One-sided Adam-Moment, or FOAM, reduces those costs by preconditioning on the input side and replacing a dense second-moment estimate with compact row and column statistics. Across models from one hundred twenty-four million to seven hundred sixty million parameters, FOAM matched strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss, used half SOAP's optimizer memory, and ran at Muon-class speed.

arxiv:2611.12304.text: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale. From Hao Kang and colleagues. Agent workloads put heavy and changing demands on large language model serving systems, which can leave processing nodes unbalanced and evict context that agents will reuse. Evolving Infra adapts computing resources and cache management to agent workloads, letting nodes switch between prompt processing and response generation. An online planner adjusts that split, while an agent-aware cache manager guides what to keep and transfer. In tests across coding, math, and computer-use tasks, it reduced average request latency by up to four point one times and ninety-fifth-percentile time to first token by up to fourteen times compared with NVIDIA's Dynamo.

arxiv:2611.17334.text: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding. From Ellis Brown and colleagues. Multimodal models differ in how they handle images, but past comparisons have mixed changes in data, model design, and compute. In controlled tests, researchers trained models on the same data and compared them at matched compute. A pretrained visual encoder was no better than one trained from scratch alongside the language model, but removing dedicated vision capacity hurt visual understanding. That capacity worked just as well inside early layers as in a separate encoder, and could make responses start sooner.

arxiv:2611.16409.text: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement. From Doyoung Kim and colleagues. Reinforcement learning often trains agents from a single reward, losing useful details such as error logs. Experience-sharing systems pass lessons between attempts, but usually do not train the model to choose those lessons. This work trains one model to act, reflect on what happened, and write task-specific playbooks, while measuring how those playbooks affect later attempts. Across agent benchmarks, the method achieves higher performance on held-out tasks than baseline methods, showing the value of learning what future attempts inherit.

arxiv:2611.13885.text: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable? From Ömer Tekin Yavuz. Neuron interventions can change a model's answer, but that does not show whether every neuron matters or whether the effect generalizes. This study tests every subset of twelve selected neurons and compares interventions across questions and relation chains. Often, only a few neurons are needed, and different subsets can produce the same answer shift. The effect carries over to rephrasings, but is much weaker on other chains, so a successful intervention does not establish a broadly transferable circuit.

arxiv:2611.16009.text: JustRUA: A Controlled Study of GPT-6 Robot-Use Agents. From Zefan Wang and colleagues. Robot-use systems have improved quickly, but different harnesses and tests make it hard to know what drives their gains. JustRUA tests key design choices in one framework, including how the model receives scene geometry and reuses past experience. A lean harness that preserves the full episode history and ends each motion early performs much better. On RoboDojo, it raises the score from 29.7 to 50.3 without a learned policy, self-improvement loop, or task-specific tuning.

arxiv:2611.16728.text: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming. From Yaru Niu and colleagues. Robots differ in their bodies, sensors, and controls, making it hard to learn from demonstrations by people, robots, and simulations together. EgoX organizes these examples by matching related observations and actions, then pretrains a shared model with separate modules for each embodiment. A training objective also asks the model to predict future visual and body-state features. Across five tasks and six robot embodiments, pretraining raised average task progress from zero point six three to zero point eight zero, with larger gains in unfamiliar conditions.

arxiv:2611.16517.text: UniSpark: Exploring Hybrid Attention for Multimodal Understanding and Generation. From Jiancheng Pan and colleagues. UniSpark tackles the challenge of combining visual understanding and image generation in one model. It pairs standard attention, which connects tokens directly, with a more compact form of attention, and trains the model to answer questions, create and edit images, and produce text alongside images. Its results include a score of 2470.3 on MME-S and 0.83 on GenEval. The work also shows examples of video creation and editing.

arxiv:2611.17256.text: Structure-Preserving Integrators for Locally Conformally Symplectic Systems: Variational Methods and Globalization. From Ayten Gezici and colleagues. Locally conformally symplectic systems can look symplectic in separate coordinate charts, but those local descriptions may not fit together into one global form. This work develops a variational method for building numerical integrators whose local steps agree when charts overlap. When they do, the local maps combine into a global map that preserves the system's geometric structure up to a discrete conformal factor. The method covers Gauss–Legendre and implicit midpoint schemes, and numerical examples demonstrate compatibility, convergence, and conformal preservation.

arxiv:2611.16835.text: Explicit Edit Codes via Multicoloring. From Huiling Xie and colleagues. Correcting insertions, deletions, and substitutions usually requires extra symbols, and explicit codes need to keep that overhead small. This work uses a prime-based multicoloring of a graph that captures which words could be confused by edits, then appends a protected representation of a color to each word. Because each word can receive several colors, the choice of color can carry message information. For fixed alphabet size and error count, the resulting codes match the leading redundancy term of a classical existential bound.

arxiv:2611.16209.text: Fréchet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression. From Jiaye Chen and colleagues. Regression often involves predictors or outcomes that are objects such as matrices, distributions, or networks, rather than ordinary numbers. Fréchet oblique forests handle these data with directional splits in metric spaces and choose splits using pairwise outcome distances, without repeatedly computing Fréchet means. Their predictions combine the weights from many trees, and the work establishes conditions for reliable performance. Tests across several types of data, including taxi-flow networks, show competitive predictive results.

arxiv:2611.16928.text: STEALTH: Steganographic Text Encoding Agnostic to Low-Level Tensor Hardware. From William Fleshman. Text-based secret-message systems often fail if the sender and receiver compute a language model's token probabilities even slightly differently. STEALTH uses keyed random noise to choose tokens, then a rateless code to recover messages despite some decoding errors, without requiring the two sides to agree exactly on probabilities. The work proves its stegotexts remain indistinguishable from ordinary model output. In tests, it decoded every message across changes in precision, hardware, and even model families, while resisting the tested detection methods.

arxiv:2611.17005.text: An Integrated Architecture for Data-Efficient Real-Time Neural Imitation of Nonlinear Time-Optimal Model Predictive Control. From Maarten De Baecke and colleagues. Nonlinear time-optimal control can produce fast, capable controllers, but solving it is too costly for real-time use on fast systems. This work trains a neural network to imitate a long-horizon controller with hard terminal constraints, and combines targeted expert queries with methods to handle data quality, changing inputs, constraints, and model mismatch. Its sampling method reaches standard performance in about one-third of the training time, using less than half the data. On a real Furuta pendulum, the controller matches the expert's region of attraction and raises control frequency from one point four hertz to one kilohertz.

arxiv:2611.16614.text: Nonsense nonlinear correlations between independent random walks. From Liping Zhu and colleagues. Sample distance correlation can look strong even when two random walks are independent, making standard tests misleading. For walks whose steps are independent, identically distributed, centred, and have finite positive variance, the study proves that their correlation approaches a universal random limit based on two independent Brownian paths. That limit can take values throughout the interval from zero to one. Ordinary permutation tests wrongly reject independence with probability tending to one, a failure also illustrated in simulations.

arxiv:2611.16657.text: Price co-movement and price information diverge across Nordic electricity zones after the energy crisis. From My Thi Diem Phan and colleagues. Nordic electricity prices have become less synchronized with German prices since the energy crisis, but it is unclear whether this also changes what information prices carry. The study measured price co-movement from 2018 to 2025 and tested a single forecasting model across Norwegian and Swedish zones. Nearby prices improved forecasts only slightly, regardless of how closely zones moved with Germany. Wind and solar forecasts mattered much more in Sweden and Germany than in Norway, showing that continental price links do not reveal where renewable forecasts are most useful.

arxiv:2611.16961.text: The Value of Thinking: Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models. From Zhengxu Yu and colleagues. Many models either shorten their written reasoning or skip it, but still produce every answer token by token. A hybrid decision model uses one frozen model for both a fast answer and full reasoning, with a small routing block that decides whether extra thinking is worth its cost. For tasks without labels for each decision, a training method learns the routing policy from episode-level results. On JevBench, the model scored slightly higher than Jev while taking less time, and on MiniWoB it cut token costs by eighty point one percent.

arxiv:2611.16321.text: From Large Language Models to Efficient System One Models via Adaptive Computation. From Minh-Anh Nguyen. Turning a large language model into a decision system can be costly because every decision uses the full network, even when fewer layers might suffice. The work finds that decision information is concentrated in the middle layers, and that the final six layers can be removed without loss. It then trains one model with shorter versions that share computation, plus a gate that decides when to use more layers. Across seven benchmarks, this approach matches or beats separately trained models at every depth and improves the balance between accuracy and efficiency.

arxiv:2611.17086.text: Partition of Unity Data-driven Finite Element Method for Anisotropic Diffusion in Magnetized Plasmas. From Siu Wun Cheung and colleagues. Simulating heat and particle transport in magnetized plasmas is difficult because diffusion along magnetic fields can far exceed diffusion across them, creating sharp boundary layers that standard finite element methods may miss. The Partition of Unity Data-Driven Finite Element Method builds local models from simulated examples of magnetic fields and boundary conditions, then combines their key patterns into a global approximation. The resulting basis can be reused across different magnetic field configurations, reducing the online computational work needed for large-scale plasma simulations.

arxiv:2611.15635.text: An Empirical Square-Root Law for the Degree Discrepancy of Binary m-Sequences. From Joonas Pääkkönen. Binary maximum-length sequences can have uneven degree counts across different windows, but the size and location of the worst imbalance are unclear. Profiles computed for every sequence size up to two to the twenty-eighth suggest that the largest discrepancy grows like the square root of the sequence size. The measured peaks oscillate between about half and one times that scale, while windows near the midpoint still show large discrepancies. The worst window does not reliably occur near the midpoint, so its location is not part of the proposed scaling law.

arxiv:2611.17273.text: Unequal-probability distributional balance and the Horvitz-Thompson estimator. From Blair Robertson and colleagues. When the link between study outcomes and auxiliary information is unclear, it can be hard to choose variables that improve estimates under probability sampling. This method balances the sample's auxiliary distribution against a population distribution weighted by the prescribed inclusion probabilities. Under a stated regularity condition, the authors bound the variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator using the expected energy distance. Their unit-swapping algorithm preserves the required inclusion probabilities and is tested on generated populations and Meuse data.

arxiv:2611.16890.text: Look It Up: Multi-bit LLM Watermarking via Codebook Search. From Jarosław Janas and colleagues. Attributing short language-model texts to a specific source is difficult when watermarking needs long outputs or slow decoding. This method encodes a short payload as a longer codeword, biases token choices during generation, then finds the closest match in a secret codebook. It recovered payloads almost perfectly for sixteen- to twenty-four-bit messages in two-hundred-token texts, with strong results in shorter texts from base models. Very short outputs from some instruction-tuned models were less reliable, and heavier rewrites remained hard to handle.

arxiv:2611.16524.text: A Joint LLM and Optimization Agent Solution for Drone Scheduling in Victim Search Missions. From Yinghao Zhang and colleagues. Searching for moving victims in wilderness areas is difficult because drone detections are uncertain and each aircraft has limited energy. The proposed system uses a ground-control agent to coordinate several drones over repeated search cycles. A large language model reasons about where to search, while an optimizer decides how to dispatch the drones within their energy limits. In simulations, the system consistently completed the mission; none of six non-language-model baselines did, and direct language-model scheduling was considerably less reliable.

arxiv:2611.15442.text: Sharp Gaussian approximation for Polyak, Ruppert averaged linear stochastic approximation. From Bogdan Butyrin and colleagues. Polyak–Ruppert averaging can make linear stochastic approximation behave like a Gaussian, but how quickly that approximation becomes accurate depends on the step size. For bounded, independent and identically distributed coefficients, the study proves that the error over convex sets is of order n to the power gamma minus one, for step sizes that decay as k to the power minus gamma. A matching lower bound shows this rate cannot be improved for any fixed model. The fastest rate is one over the square root of n, and the recursive multiplier bootstrap achieves that same error bound.

arxiv:2611.14938.text: When Does a Recommendation Spark Curiosity? Theory, Measurement, and Field Evidence. From Pan Li and colleagues. Recommendation systems often show people more of what they already like, which can limit discovery and curiosity. This work turns the information-gap theory of curiosity into a measurable score for how much a recommended item makes someone want to know more. In a survey, the score matched people's reported curiosity better than other measures, and offline tests across three datasets showed that recommendations using it outperformed existing methods. A large online trial at an Asian video platform increased clicks, video views, and time spent, and the system remains in use.

arxiv:2611.15094.text: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging. From Chenhui Zhao and colleagues. Interpreting full brain scans and explaining what they mean for care remains difficult for artificial intelligence. Neuro-VL was trained on nearly one million scans from routine clinical care to interpret complete examinations and discuss findings in everyday language. Across internal and international datasets, it outperformed general-purpose and specialized medical models at finding, locating, and describing abnormalities, and writing reports. It also compared scans over time and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions, pointing toward AI that can support ongoing disease monitoring.

arxiv:2611.11306.text: ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping. From Joseph Marvin Imperial and colleagues. Web-scraping agents can violate website rules and laws, but their ability to follow those rules has been hard to measure. ScrapeBench tests whether AI agents follow terms of service and robots.txt directives across websites that allow or prohibit scraping. Most agents complied in fewer than five percent of cases when scraping was prohibited, even when they checked the rules. On sites that allowed scraping, some agents refused anyway; people also over-refused, while following rules at rates comparable to AI agents.

arxiv:2611.14883.text: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions. From Xiangjian Zhang and colleagues. Reconstructing an obstacle in a mean-field game from observations of its value function is difficult, especially on irregular domains and in high dimensions. This method combines policy iteration with fixed random features, turning each step into linear least-squares problems based on sampled points rather than a mesh. It can use different representations for the obstacle, value function, and population density, and enforce boundary conditions on irregular domains. Tests with smooth and discontinuous obstacles, domains with holes, and higher-dimensional problems show accurate results and flexibility.

arxiv:2611.15393.text: VR-Net: Subarray-Level Inter-Cell Coordination for Multi-Cell XL-MIMO under Near-Field Spatial Non-Stationarity. From Muhammad Shoaib Ayub and colleagues. In near-field multi-cell systems with extremely large antennas, each user is visible to only part of each array, making full coordination costly. VR-Net uses these visibility regions to coordinate beamforming between relevant subarrays and limit the channel information that stations must share. In simulations, it kept at least ninety-nine point six percent of the full-array method's sum rate while sending ten to thirty-nine percent fewer channel entries. Coordination also improved performance by up to thirty-three percent over designing each cell independently.
